entity.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
entity.description: Russian novelist who survived a mock execution and Siberian hard labor to write Crime and Punishment, The Brothers Karamazov, and The Idiot — the deepest explorations of guilt, faith, and human psychology in literature.

story.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
story.description: Born at a Moscow hospital for the poor, arrested for reading banned books, sentenced to death then reprieved at the last second, and exiled to Siberia — then wrote the greatest novels in the Russian language.

moments.name: Dostoevsky Is Born at a Moscow Hospital for the Poor
moments.subtitle: The future novelist grows up among patients at the bottom of the Russian social scale
moments.description: On 11 November 1821 (30 October Old Style), Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was born in Moscow, the second child of Dr. Mikhail Dostoevsky and Maria Dostoevskaya. The family lived in quarters on the grounds of the Mariinsky Hospital for the Poor, where Dostoevsky's father worked as a physician. The young Fyodor played in the hospital gardens alongside patients from the lowest rungs of Russian society — an experience that shaped his lifelong empathy for the suffering and dispossessed. His mother taught him to read using the Bible, and his nanny read him fairy tales from age three. The hospital building, now a museum, still stands on Dostoevsky Street in Moscow.

moments.name: Dostoevsky Publishes Poor Folk and Is Hailed as a Literary Genius at 24
moments.subtitle: Russia's leading critic declares the unknown author has written the first "social novel"
moments.description: On 15 January 1846, Fyodor Dostoevsky's first novel, Poor Folk, was published in the St Petersburg Collection almanac. The manuscript had reached the influential critic Vissarion Belinsky through a chain of literary friends; Belinsky declared it Russia's first "social novel" and hailed the unknown 24-year-old as a major talent. The epistolary novel about a poor copying clerk and a young seamstress became a commercial success and gained Dostoevsky instant entry into Saint Petersburg's literary circles. The triumph was so sudden that Dostoevsky resigned his military engineering post to pursue writing full-time — a decision that would lead to both artistic greatness and decades of financial ruin.

moments.name: Dostoevsky Begins Four Years of Hard Labor in a Siberian Prison Camp
moments.subtitle: Shackled in leg irons, the novelist shares barracks with murderers and thieves
moments.description: In January 1850, Fyodor Dostoevsky arrived at the Omsk prison camp in western Siberia to begin a four-year sentence of hard labor. After his death sentence for membership in the Petrashevsky Circle was commuted at the last moment, Dostoevsky was stripped of his civil rights and sent to one of Russia's harshest penal colonies. Shackled in leg irons, sharing barracks with convicted murderers, Dostoevsky endured brutal conditions that would later inspire The House of the Dead (1860-1862). Upon release in 1854, he faced six more years of compulsory military service in exile. The experience transformed Dostoevsky's worldview, deepening his Orthodox faith and his obsession with suffering and redemption.

moments.name: Dostoevsky Writes Crime and Punishment in a Desperate Race Against Debt
moments.subtitle: A gambling addict produces the greatest psychological novel ever written to pay his creditors
moments.description: In 1866, Fyodor Dostoevsky published Crime and Punishment in serial form in the Russian literary journal The Russian Messenger while living in Saint Petersburg. Dostoevsky was deeply in debt from gambling losses and had signed a punishing contract with a publisher that would have forfeited all rights to his works if he missed his deadline. He hired a stenographer, Anna Snitkina, and dictated large sections of the novel at frantic speed. The story of Raskolnikov, a student who murders a pawnbroker and is consumed by guilt, became the defining work of psychological fiction. Dostoevsky married Anna Snitkina the following year — she would manage his finances and save him from ruin.

moments.name: Dostoevsky Dies in Saint Petersburg Two Months After Finishing The Brothers Karamazov
moments.subtitle: Thirty thousand mourners follow the coffin of the greatest Russian novelist
moments.description: On 9 February 1881 (28 January Old Style), Fyodor Dostoevsky died of a pulmonary hemorrhage at his apartment in Saint Petersburg at the age of 59. He had completed The Brothers Karamazov, widely considered his masterwork and one of the supreme achievements of world literature, just months earlier in November 1880. An estimated 30,000 mourners followed his funeral procession through the streets of Saint Petersburg to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery, where he was buried. Nietzsche later called Dostoevsky the only psychologist from whom he had something to learn. His novels have since been translated into more than 170 languages.
